Stewart, Calculus: Early Transcendentals · Section 15.7 · Exercise 46

Moment of Inertia of a Solid Cone about Its Axis

Problem

Assume that the solid has constant density k. Find the moment of inertia about the z-axis of the solid cone x2+y2​≤z≤h.

Reading the solid

The lower surface is the cone z=x2+y2​, which opens upward from the origin. The upper surface is the horizontal plane z=h. The two surfaces meet where h=x2+y2​, that is, on the circle of radius h in the plane z=h. The solid is a cone of height h whose base radius also equals h.

Cylindrical coordinates fit the rotational symmetry. Put x=rcosθ and y=rsinθ. Then x2+y2=r2, so the cone surface is simply z=r and the solid is described by

r≤z≤h,0≤r≤h,0≤θ≤2π.

The volume element is dV=rdzdrdθ. The factor r is the circumference of the shell at radius r.

Every point of the solid at radius r has distance r from the z-axis, and the perpendicular distance enters the moment of inertia as its square. The moment density is therefore kr2:

Iz​=∭E​(x2+y2)ρdV=k∭E​r2dV.

Solution

Step 1 — Set up the iterated integral

Insert the bounds and the volume element:

Iz​=k∫02π​∫0h​∫rh​r2⋅rdzdrdθ=k∫02π​∫0h​∫rh​r3dzdrdθ.

The two powers of r combine: one factor is the distance squared, and the other is the circumference factor of the shell.

Step 2 — Integrate with respect to z

The integrand does not depend on z, so the inner integral gives the height of the shell:

∫rh​r3dz=r3(h−r).

Step 3 — Integrate with respect to r

Expand the product and integrate term by term:

∫0h​r3(h−r)dr=∫0h​(hr3−r4)dr=h⋅4h4​−5h5​=h5(41​−51​)=20h5​.

Step 4 — Integrate with respect to θ

The last integral runs over a full turn:

Iz​=k∫02π​20h5​dθ=k⋅2π⋅20h5​=10πkh5​.

Step 5 — Check the answer against the mass

The mass of the cone is one third of the mass of the enclosing cylinder:

m=∭E​kdV=k∫02π​∫0h​∫rh​rdzdrdθ=2πk∫0h​r(h−r)dr=3πkh3​.

Divide the moment by the mass. The density and the height cancel in a way that shows how the moment scales:

mIz​​=πkh3/3πkh5/10​=103h2​,Iz​=103​mh2.

The factor 3/10 lies between the value 1 for a thin hoop of radius h and the value 0 for a point mass on the axis. That ordering is correct, because most of the mass of the cone sits close to the axis, where r is small.

Answer

Iz​=10πkh5​=103​mh2,m=3πkh3​.

Notation

SymbolMeaning
kThe constant density of the solid, in mass per unit volume.
z=x2+y2​The cone surface: its height above the xy-plane equals the distance from the z-axis.
hThe height of the cone. The base radius also equals h, because the surface reaches z=h at r=h.
r,θ,zCylindrical coordinates: r is the distance from the z-axis, θ the angle in the xy-plane, z the height.
dVThe volume element rdzdrdθ. The extra factor r appears because a shell of radius r has circumference 2πr.
Iz​The moment of inertia about the z-axis, ∭(x2+y2)ρdV. It measures resistance to rotation about that axis.
mThe mass of the solid, ∭ρdV.
shellThe thin cylindrical wall of radius r, thickness dr, and height h−r that the integral adds up.

Verification

Three scripts confirm the result.

  • part1_step1.py integrates the shell form 2πkr3(h−r) with mpmath at h=1, k=1 and obtains 0.314159265358979, which equals π/10. It also samples four million points in the enclosing cylinder and reports 0.314157, a deviation of −0.01 standard errors from π/10.
  • part1_step2.py repeats the derivation in SymPy. It prints kr3(h−r) after the z-integral, h5k/20 after the r-integral, and πh5k/10 after the θ-integral. It also confirms m=πh3k/3 and Iz​/m=3h2/10.
  • part1_step3.py repeats the quadrature at h=2 and k=3. It obtains 30.159289474462 from both the quadrature and the closed form, and the same value from 3mh2/10. The relative difference is below 10−25.
